partes.p: In the variants of the Solow model we have seen so far, we assumed the production function featured constant returns to scale in capital and labor. This assumption might be violated in practice if there are scarce factors, such as land or natural resources, that also affect production. This exercise develops a version of the Solow model with scarce factors. We do this using a variant of the Solow model in continuous time analyzed in the first part of Lecture 6. Suppose output is now given by
$$Y (t) =\text{ AK}(t)^{\alpha}L(t)^{\beta}Z^{1-\alpha -\beta}$$

where $\alpha + \beta < 1$. Here, $Z$ can be interpreted as the supply of the scarce factors such as land. The coefficient, 1 $- \alpha - \beta > 0$, can be interpreted as the share (or the "importance") of the scarce factors in aggregate output. Unlike $K(t)$ and $L(t)$, scarce factors cannot be accumulated—at least not as easily. We capture this feature by assuming that $Z$ is constant. To simplify the notation we also adopt the normalization $Z = 1$, so that output is given by
$$Y (t) =\text{ AK}(t)^{\alpha}L(t)^{\beta}$$
The rest of the model is as before. Specifically, the dynamics of capital and labor are respectively given by,
$$\dot{K}(t) =\text{ sY }(t) - \delta K(t)$$
$$\dot{L}(t) = L(t)n$$
for some constants $s$ ∈ (0,$1), \delta > 0$ and $n \geq 0$, and taking initial values $K(0)$ and $L(0)$ as given.

(3)-(4) can be combined to describe the dynamics of the model in terms of capital per labor, $k(t) = K(t)$/L$(t)$ and output per labor, $y(t) = Y (t)$/L$(t)$. Carry out this analysis and show that the following equation continues to hold in this setting,
$$\dot{k}(t) =\text{ sy}(t) - (\delta + n)k(t)$$

partes.p: Combining your analysis from the first two parts, obtain a diferential equation that features only $k(t)$ and the parameters of the model (including $L)$. Characterize the steady state level of capital and output per labor, $k$ and $y$. How does a greater population level, $L$, affect $k$? How does it affect $y$? Is the proportional effect$^{2}$ on $y$ the same as, greater than, or smaller than the proportional effect on $y(t)$ that you analyzed in part b)? Provide an intuition for this result.

In the variants of the Solow model we have seen so far, the population was either constant, or it was growing at a constant rate, which did not affect the behavior of per-labor variables very much. This exercise analyzes a model in which population growth responds to changes in output per labor, an idea that was emphasized by Thomas Malthus more than 200 years ago. We also assume there are scarce factors in production, as in the first exercise. Specifically, consider the model in the first exercise with the only difference that popula tion growth is now given by
$$n(t) = \frac{\dot{L}(t)}{L(t)} = \eta (y(t) - \bar{y})$$
where $\bar{y} > 0, \eta > 0$, and $L(0)$ is given. The rest of the model is unchanged. In particular, we continue to assume that the production function is given by (2) with $\alpha + \beta < 1$.

Provide an economic interpretation of (6). What happens to population growth when $y(t)$ is below $\bar{y}$ (say when $y(t)$ is close to zero)? Is this intuitive? And what happens to population growth when $y(t)$ exceeds $\bar{y}$?
$^{2}$In general, when we say proportional efect of $a$ on $b$, we consider $\frac{∂ ln b}{∂ ln a}$.

contexto.p: depends on the level of the population, $L(t)$. This implies that the dynamics of the model are now more complicated. In particular, the diferential equation (7) cannot be solved in isolation. Rather, the diferential equations (6) and (7) jointly determine the evolution of {$L(t)$, k$(t)$}, starting from an initial condition, {$L(0)$, k(0)}. That said, the steady state of the system is relatively less complicated. In the rest of this exercise, we focus on a steady state in which $L(t) = L^{*} > 0$ and $k(t) = k^{*} > 0$ for each $t$.

partes.p: In lectures, we have seen that output per labor (or more broadly, the living standards) remained roughly unchanged for much of the human history (until the Industrial Revolu tion), even though there has been technological progress along the way. Use your analysis in c) to provide an interpretation for this fact.

Consider the neoclassical growth model in continuous time. Output per labor is given by $y(t) = f (k(t))$, where $f ($•) is a neoclassical production function and $k(t)$ denotes the capital per labor. There is no population growth or technological progress (that is, $\dot{L/L} = 0$ and $\dot{A/A} = 0)$. We now also introduce government spending to the model, denoted by $g(t)$. The economy's resource constraint is given by:
$$\dot{k}(t) = f (k(t)) - \delta k(t) - c(t) - g(t)$$

The representative household has per-period utility $u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\theta}-1}{1-\theta}$ and discount rate $\rho$ . The economy is initially (at time $t = 0)$ at the steady state corresponding to $g^{old}(t) = 0$. Denote the consumption and capital per labor at this old steady-state with {$c^{*,old}$, k$^{*,old}$}. At time 0, Congress approves an increase in military spending. The announcement comes as a surprise. After the announcement, the government spending is $g^{new}(t) = \bar{g} > 0$ for each $t \geq 0$. Hence, the government spending increases permanently. For the purposes of this exercise, you can think of the government spending as purely wasteful (as it will be spent outside the country). Furthermore suppose that government spending is not too large, so that it satisfies $\bar{g}$ < f$(k^{*,old}) - \delta k^{*,old}$. First suppose government spending is financed by taking resources lump-sum from con sumers (i.e., a lump-sum tax), so that the Euler equation is not affected by the change.

Characterize the new steady-state levels of consumption per labor and capital per labor, {$c^{*,new}$, k$^{*,new}$}. How do the new steady-state levels, {$c^{*,new}$, k$^{*,new}$}, compare with the old steady-state levels, {$c^{*,old}$, k$^{*,old}$}? Provide a brief intuition.
Draw the phase diagram and show how the economy transitions to the new steady-state. What is the impact on consumption per labor and capital per labor in the short run? What about the long run?

In this problem you will explore the implications of the subsidy under different assumptions on its tax financing.

(i) What does the government budget constraint imply about the relationship between $\tau_{t}, \chi , r_{t}$, and $k_{t}$? [Hint: the tax revenue that the government collects from households will need to be equal to the amount that it is paying out as subsidies to firms.] (ii) Derive the optimality conditions for the household and firm problem. Combining those optimality conditions with (i) the household budget constraint, (ii) the ex pression for firm profits, and (iii) the government budget constraint, derive a pair of difference equations that characterize the dynamic evolution of consumption $c_{t}$ and capital $k_{t}$. Compare your system with the standard planner's system
$$\frac{c_{t}^{-\theta}}{\beta c_{t+1}^{-\theta}} = 1 - \delta + f'(k_{t+1})$$

Is it different? If so, why? (iii) Does $\chi$ affect the steady-state levels of capital $k^{*}$ and consumption $c^{*}$? If so, how? In particular, is it possible that $k^{*}$ exceeds the golden rule level of the capital stock? (iv) Suppose that the economy is initially at steady state. Then, at $t = 0$, the subsidy $\chi$ is unexpectedly and permanently removed (i.e., we go from $\chi > 0$ to $\chi = 0)$. Graphically illustrate the transition paths of capital $k(t)$ and consumption $c(t)$, using the phase diagram for the continuous-time version of the model.
